procedural_history.originating_court: Industrial Tribunal, Delhi (Sri Ram Kanwar, Industrial Tribunal)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated April 17, 1954, made by the Industrial Tribunal, Delhi, directing the appellant (Punjab National Bank) to pay travelling and halting allowances to the representatives of various Unions (other than the two located in Delhi) to attend the hearing before the Tribunal in Delhi.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant (Punjab National Bank) moved the Punjab High Court for a writ of certiorari to quash the order of the Industrial Tribunal. The Punjab High Court dismissed the petition in limine (i.e., without a full hearing) on May 14, 1954.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant (Punjab National Bank) obtained special leave from the Supreme Court on October 18, 1954, to appeal the decision of the Punjab High Court.

directions: The costs must be paid by the contesting respondents.

issue.issue_text: Whether an Industrial Tribunal has the discretionary power under Section 11(7) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, to direct a party to pay the travelling and halting allowances of the representatives of another party during a pending proceeding, irrespective of the final outcome.

facts: During a pending dispute between a bank and its workmen, the workmen's unions applied to the Industrial Tribunal for an order.
The unions requested that the bank be directed to pay the travelling and halting allowances for their representatives attending the proceedings in Delhi from other cities.
The Tribunal granted the order, not based on a specific law, but on what it considered the "general practice" of Industrial Courts.
The bank appealed this order to the Supreme Court, arguing that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to make such an order.
law: The central legal provision is Section 11(7) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, which states that the costs of any proceeding shall be at the discretion of the Tribunal.
The Court clarified that this discretion is a "judicial discretion" and must be exercised according to the "rules of reason and justice," not based on caprice, private opinion, or sympathy.
Orders for costs, even under the wide wording of Section 11(7), must be made on "well-recognised principles."
application: The Court first rejected the Tribunal's reliance on "general practice," stating that there was no uniform or consistent practice in this matter.
It further held that even if such a practice existed, it was "neither warranted by law nor by the principles of reason and justice."

The Court then interpreted Section 11(7) and found that, on a proper construction, it does not grant the Tribunal the power to direct one party to pay the costs of another party in advance, irrespective of the final result of the proceeding.
The Court explicitly disapproved of a previous decision (*Certain Banking Companies v. Their Workmen*) that had allowed such payments, finding its reasoning unsustainable.
Conversely, the Court approved of the view in *Jeevan Textile Mills, Hyderabad (Deccan) v. Their Workmen*, which held that costs must be awarded based on established principles.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the Industrial Tribunal's order was without jurisdiction. It held that the discretionary power to award costs under Section 11(7) of the Industrial Disputes Act does not include the power to compel a party to pay the travelling and halting allowances of another party's representatives during a pending proceeding, before the final outcome is determined.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an Industrial Tribunal has the discretionary power under Section 11(7) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, to direct a party to pay the travelling and halting allowances of the representatives of another party during a pending proceeding, irrespective of the final outcome.
appellant_arguments: The order passed by the Industrial Tribunal was wholly without jurisdiction and unjust.

On a plain reading of Section 11(7), the expression 'costs of any proceeding' means costs of the entire proceeding as determined on its conclusion, not costs to be incurred in the future by a party in a pending proceeding.
The expression 'costs incidental to any proceeding' similarly means costs of interlocutory applications that have been determined at their conclusion, not costs payable in advance.
Neither of the expressions in the sub-section refers to halting and travelling allowances to be incurred by a party while attending the Court on his own behalf.
respondent_arguments: The concluding portion of Section 11(7), which allows for the recovery of costs 'as arrears of land revenue', shows that costs may be granted in advance during a pending proceeding.
An Industrial Tribunal becomes functus officio after submitting its award.
The sub-section states that an application for recovery of costs can be made to 'it' (interpreted by the respondent as the Tribunal).
Therefore, the application for costs must be made before the Tribunal becomes functus officio, meaning while the proceeding is still pending.

cases.case_name: Jeevan Textile Mills, Hyderabad (Deccan) v. Their Workmen
cases.principle: The discretion given to a Tribunal under s. 11(7) of the Industrial Disputes Act is a judicial discretion and must be exercised according to the rules of reason and justice, not by chance or caprice or private opinion.

cases.case_name: Certain Banking Companies v. Their Workmen
cases.principle: The Court disapproved of the principle decided in this case, which was that a Tribunal had the power and jurisdiction under s. 11(7) of the Act to direct Banks to meet the expenses of the workmen in a pending proceeding.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An Industrial Tribunal's discretion under sub-section (7) of section 11 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, is a judicial discretion that must be exercised according to the rules of reason and justice. This power does not permit the Tribunal to direct one party to pay the costs of another party in advance of and irrespective of the final result of the proceeding. The expression "costs of any proceeding" refers to the costs of the entire proceeding as determined upon its conclusion, not costs to be incurred in the future by a party.
obiter: The general rule is that costs follow the event unless the Court, for good reasons, otherwise orders.

The principle that a richer party must pay the expenses of a weaker party, irrespective of the ultimate result, would encourage frivolous disputes and run counter to the promotion of industrial peace.
The practice in English Matrimonial Courts regarding securing a wife's costs stands on a special footing governed by special statutory provisions and has no application to industrial disputes.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: An Industrial Tribunal has no power, in the exercise of its discretion under Section 11(7) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, to direct one party to pay the travelling and halting allowances of the representatives of another party in a pending proceeding and irrespective of its final outcome. Such an order is a negation of justice and reason, as the discretion granted must be a judicial one, and the general rule is that costs follow the event unless the court, for good reasons, orders otherwise.
legal_tests_applied: Statutory Interpretation of Section 11(7): The court performed a 'plain reading' of the expressions 'costs of any proceeding' and 'costs incidental to any proceeding' to determine their meaning and scope.

Judicial Discretion: The court applied the principle that statutory discretion must be a 'judicial discretion' and 'exercised according to the rules of reason and justice, not by chance or caprice or private opinion or some fanciful idea of benevolence or sympathy.'
Costs Follow the Event: The court relied on the general rule that costs are awarded based on the final outcome of the proceeding.
policy_considerations: Forcing a financially stronger party to pay the expenses of a weaker party, irrespective of the ultimate result, would 'encourage frivolous and unsubstantial disputes' and run counter to the Act's purpose of promoting industrial peace.

'Social justice' does not mean that reason and fairness must always yield to the convenience of one party at the cost of the other, as such a 'one-sided or partial view is really next of kin to caprice or humour.'

The principles of natural justice cannot be invoked to support an order that penalises one party by making it pay for the costs of the other party in advance, as such an order is 'neither natural nor has any element of justice in it.'

Judicial discretion must be exercised 'according to the rules of reason and justice, not according to private opinion : Rooke's Case (1 ) ; according to law, and not humour. It is to be, not arbitrary, vague, and fanciful, but legal and regular.'
